beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Supriya and this video is about SQL query optimization for analytics. Two queries, identical output: the same four thousand four hundred fifty-nine rows. One reads eleven thousand rows to get there. The other reads four hundred thousand. The SQL won't tell you which. The query plan will.

the ask types itself into the composer, character by character
send button arms (terracotta); runningText 'reading the plan…' appears
RESULT line 1 lands — 'A → SCAN postings'
RESULT line 2 lands — 'B → SEARCH … USING INDEX'
RESULT line 3 lands — '35× fewer rows read'; the ask is answered on screen

props.command: I have a 400,000-row postings table with an index on posted_at. Two queries return identical results — one filters with strftime('%Y-%m', posted_at) = '2026-01', the other with posted_at >= '2026-01-01' AND posted_at < '2026-02-01'. Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on both and tell me which one can use the index, and why.

beats.narration_text: Here is the shape of a typical analytics query. Four hundred thousand postings. You want one month: eleven thousand rows survive the filter, and grouping by account leaves four thousand four hundred fifty-nine. Optimization is about how many of the four hundred thousand the database has to touch.

surviving dots migrate to panel 3, collapsing to 4; counter '1% remain'
the 4 final dots turn terracotta — the only accent in the frame

props.command: Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on both queries against demo/postings.db and show me the two plans side by side, unedited.

beats.narration_text: There it is. Query A: SCAN postings. Scan means every row, all four hundred thousand. Query B: SEARCH postings USING INDEX, with the date range in the parentheses. Search means the index walked to January and stopped. Same answer, and the plan said so before either query ran.

card A's verdict strip draws in — '400,000 rows read'

card B's verdict strip draws in — '11,369 rows read'; citation line settles bottom-left

left.heading: A — non-sargable
left.code:
sqlite> EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
  SELECT account_id, SUM(amount_cents)
  FROM postings
  WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', posted_at) = '2026-01'
  GROUP BY account_id;

QUERY PLAN
|--SCAN postings
`--USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY

right.heading: B — sargable
right.code:
sqlite> EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
  SELECT account_id, SUM(amount_cents)
  FROM postings
  WHERE posted_at >= '2026-01-01'
    AND posted_at <  '2026-02-01'
  GROUP BY account_id;

QUERY PLAN
|--SEARCH postings USING INDEX
|    idx_postings_posted_at (posted_at>? AND posted_at<?)
`--USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY

beats.narration_text: Before I show you why, commit to an answer. Both queries filter on the same indexed column. So what is it about Query A's WHERE clause that takes the index away?

show.event: the predict card rises on the cream stage; spark line top

props.question: Both filter the same indexed column. What does A's WHERE clause do that costs it the index?
props.commit: commit — the answer is one beat away

beats.narration_text: The function. Query A wraps the posted-at column in strftime, so the database has an expression instead of a column, and evaluating it means visiting every row. Query B leaves the column bare. That is the insight: a plain index works on the column, not on a function of the column.

the upper track bends DOWN; its label sets as strftime(…) = '2026-01'

track B rises; notes stack in — 'bare column, range predicate' / 'index seek'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Before you tune a query, run EXPLAIN and look for the word SCAN. If it shows up on a table you thought was indexed, check your WHERE clause for a function wrapped around the indexed column, like strftime, CAST or UPPER, and compare the bare column instead. That one move took four hundred thousand rows down to eleven thousand.

props.artifactTitle: SQL, Read Fewer Rows — one page
artifactLines: EXPLAIN costs almost nothing and does not run your query — read the plan before you tune anything.
SCAN means every row. SEARCH … USING INDEX means the engine got to skip rows.
A function around an indexed column (strftime, CAST, UPPER) makes a plain index unusable.
Compare the bare column instead: 400,000 rows read became 11,369 — same 4,459 rows out.
